lead: An optical fibre is a glass or plastic thread that carries light along its length. It works by total internal reflection: light in a core of higher refractive index bounces off a cladding of lower refractive index. This keeps the ray inside the core for kilometres. Fibres carry internet and phone traffic, connect sensors, and make images in endoscopes. The key numbers are the critical angle, the numerical aperture and the acceptance angle. They tell how tightly light is trapped and how much light the fibre can gather.
prereq: You need refraction and total internal reflection (see Unit 4, Wave Optics) and the idea of an electromagnetic wave (see Unit 3, Electromagnetism and Maxwell's Equations).

sections.h3: The core, the cladding and total internal reflection

blocks.text: The core is the central glass or plastic path that carries light. Its refractive index is n1. The cladding surrounds the core and has a lower refractive index n2. A plastic buffer covers the cladding for mechanical protection. The outer jacket protects the whole cable from moisture, abrasion and bending. Only the core and cladding guide light.

Total internal reflection happens at the core–cladding boundary when light travels from the denser core to the rarer cladding. Measure the angle of incidence θ<sub>i</sub> from the normal to the boundary. At the critical angle θ<sub>c</sub>, the refracted ray grazes along the boundary. For θ<sub>i</sub> > θ<sub>c</sub>, no light crosses into the cladding; the ray reflects back into the core. This is total internal reflection.

blocks.where: θ<sub>c</sub> is the critical angle measured from the normal at the core–cladding boundary; n<sub>1</sub> is the core refractive index; n<sub>2</sub> is the cladding refractive index. The formula needs n<sub>1</sub> > n<sub>2</sub>.

blocks.text: A ray launched too steeply hits the boundary below θ<sub>c</sub> and leaks out. A ray launched within the fibre's acceptance cone stays guided. The core must have n<sub>1</sub> > n<sub>2</sub>; if the cladding index is higher, total internal reflection cannot occur at the core boundary.

A meridional ray is a ray that travels in a plane containing the fibre axis. It crosses the axis after each reflection. Consider such a ray entering the flat fibre end from air at angle θa to the axis. At the air–core face, Snell's law gives sin θa = n1 sin θr, where θr is the angle inside the core to the axis. The ray then meets the core–cladding boundary at angle 90° − θr to the normal.

For total internal reflection, 90° − θ<sub>r</sub> ≥ θ<sub>c</sub>, so θ<sub>r</sub> ≤ 90° − θ<sub>c</sub>. The largest entry angle that is guided is θ<sub>a</sub>. Put θ<sub>r</sub> = 90° − θ<sub>c</sub> in Snell's law: sin θ<sub>a</sub> = n<sub>1</sub> cos θ<sub>c</sub> = n<sub>1</sub>√(1 − (n<sub>2</sub>/n<sub>1</sub>)<sup>2</sup>) = √(n<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup> − n<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup>). The right side is the numerical aperture.

blocks.where: NA is the numerical aperture, a dimensionless number; n<sub>1</sub> and n<sub>2</sub> are the core and cladding refractive indices. NA measures the light-gathering power of the fibre.
θ<sub>a</sub> is the acceptance half-angle in air; NA is the numerical aperture. A ray entering within this half-angle to the axis is guided.

blocks.text: NA is dimensionless. A larger NA means a wider acceptance cone and more light gathered, but it also tends to support more guided modes. A smaller NA gives tighter guidance and a narrower cone. The acceptance angle is measured in air; inside another medium, replace the air index 1 by that medium's index.

figure.caption: The core has the higher refractive index and the cladding has the lower index, so total internal reflection traps light in the core. The buffer and jacket protect the glass but do not guide light.

spec.aria: A stack of four layers from centre out: core with n1 = 1.50, cladding with n2 = 1.48, plastic buffer, and outer jacket.

examples.question: A step-index optical fibre has core refractive index n1 = 1.50 and cladding refractive index n2 = 1.48. The fibre is in air. Find (a) the critical angle at the core–cladding boundary, (b) the numerical aperture, and (c) the acceptance angle in air.
steps: The critical angle uses the ratio n2/n1: n2/n1 = 1.48/1.50 = 0.9867.
θc = sin−1(0.9867). In degrees, θc = 80.6°. The ray must hit the boundary above this angle.
Square the indices: n1² = 1.50² = 2.2500 and n2² = 1.48² = 2.1904.
examples.answer: The critical angle is 80.6°, the numerical aperture is 0.244, and the acceptance angle in air is 14.1°.
examples.check:
import math
n1 = 1.50
n2 = 1.48
theta_c = math.degrees(math.asin(n2 / n1))
NA = math.sqrt(n1**2 - n2**2)
theta_a = math.degrees(math.asin(NA))
print(f"{theta_c:.1f}")
print(f"{NA:.3f}")
print(f"{theta_a:.1f}")

traps: For the critical angle, use θc = sin⁻¹(n2/n1), not n1/n2. Swapping the indices makes the ratio n1/n2 greater than 1, and sin⁻¹ of a value above 1 does not exist — the formula then wrongly predicts a critical angle where total internal reflection cannot happen.
NA is √(n1² − n2²), not n1 − n2. The square root of a difference of squares is not the difference of the indices.
The acceptance angle is the half-angle of the cone in air. Do not call 2θa the acceptance angle unless the question asks for the full cone angle.
NA has no unit. A value like 0.24 is a ratio, not 0.24°.
The buffer and jacket do not guide light. Only the core and cladding set the critical angle and NA.

quiz.q: Define core and cladding in an optical fibre.
quiz.a: The core is the central light-carrying region with refractive index n1. The cladding surrounds it with a lower refractive index n2 and causes total internal reflection at the boundary.

quiz.q: State the condition for total internal reflection at the core–cladding boundary.
quiz.a: Light must travel in the core with n1 > n2, and the angle of incidence measured from the normal must be greater than the critical angle θc = sin−1(n2/n1).

quiz.q: Why must the cladding refractive index be lower than the core refractive index?
quiz.a: Total internal reflection needs light to go from a denser medium to a rarer medium. If n2 ≥ n1, there is no critical angle for the core–cladding boundary, so light refracts into the cladding instead of being trapped.

quiz.q: A fibre has n1 = 1.52 and n2 = 1.50. Find its numerical aperture and acceptance angle in air.
A fibre has NA = 0.30. Find its acceptance angle in air.
quiz.a: θa = sin−1(0.30) = 17.5°. Rays entering within 17.5° of the axis are guided.

quiz.q: A ray enters at θa = 20° into a fibre with NA = 0.22. Is it guided? Explain.
quiz.a: The maximum acceptance angle is sin−1(0.22) = 12.7°. The ray at 20° is outside this cone, so it is not guided and will leak into the cladding.

quiz.q: Explain why NA measures light-gathering power, and why a very large NA can be a disadvantage in a communication fibre.
quiz.a: NA = sin θa, so a larger NA gives a wider acceptance cone and gathers more light. In a communication fibre, a very large NA supports more guided modes. Different modes travel at different speeds, causing modal dispersion and limiting the bit rate over long distances.

beyond: Not for the exam. Research fibres add photonic crystal fibre, hollow-core fibre and multicore fibre. Photonic crystal fibre uses a pattern of air holes instead of a simple cladding. Hollow-core fibre guides light mostly in air, which can reduce loss and delay. Multicore fibre carries several independent channels in one glass strand. Search for photonic crystal fibre, hollow-core fibre and multicore fibre.
